raw_response:
I farm 20 mu, not very big, so I cannot gamble too much. I have done wheat and maize for many years, and around here this rotation is still the steadiest. If we are talking about my next full wheat-maize cycle in Quzhou, that means winter wheat sown in early October 2026, then summer maize planted right after wheat harvest in June 2027. I usually do not chase the highest input. I look at what worked on my own land and what the better farmers nearby are doing. Wheat needs to be kept steady, especially base fertilizer and a topdress at jointing. Maize has a very tight planting window after wheat, so I keep land prep simple and plant fast. We have well water, but pumping costs money, so I only irrigate at the key stages. Since some family members work off-farm, I arrange the work around the busy days and hire a little help only at harvest if needed.

For wheat, I will keep all 20 mu in the usual wheat-maize rotation. I plan to use a common improved wheat seed, sow in early to mid October, and put on base fertilizer before seeding. I usually apply a bit more nitrogen than the extension person says because I am afraid of wheat looking weak in spring, but I will not go too high because fertilizer is expensive. I will give one base application and one topdress around jointing, and irrigate about three times if rainfall is normal: once before winter if soil is dry, once at jointing, and once around grain filling. For maize, I will plant as soon as wheat is off the field, within a few days, because delay costs yield. I will use hybrid seed, do shallow rotary tillage or direct planting after the wheat stubble depending on machine availability, put part of the fertilizer at planting and the rest around the big flare stage, and usually irrigate once or twice if rain is short. Herbicide is worth the money because labor is tight; insecticide I use only if pressure shows up.
